newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's second city in limbo as rebels near.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's second city in limbo as rebels near.

text.p: Zaire's second city Lubumbashi is living in limbo, its life put on hold in the expectation Laurent Kabila's rebels may burst in at any moment.

The southern city has treated their arrival merely as a matter of time for three weeks now, ever since the fall of Kisangani made a military defence of President Mobutu Sese Seko's rule look like a pipe dream.
The northern jungle city's weekend capture and Kabila's vow that Lubumbashi was next frayed nerves here. Well-off citizens booked into the copper town's top hotel, the Karavia, for safety in numbers.
They soon checked out again. Perceptions of how imminent the rebel attack is have fluctuated wildly.
Panic has set in periodically on the slightest rumour, although the closest reliable sighting of a rebel has been more than 200 km (120 miles) away.

On Wednesday night, the word was the town was encircled. Restaurants shut their doors and nobody stirred on the streets but soldiers. By Thursday, the danger had gone puff into thin air and things livened up again, a bit.
"I just hope we can get this phase over with as fast as possible. It's unbearable and it is deathly for trade," said one senior employee at the Karavia.
The hotel, usually teeming with businessmen attracted by the area's rich mining potential and new openness to foreign investors, has guests in only five of its 200 bedrooms.
Foreigners close to military and community leaders in Lubumbashi say the rebels, their path aided by militant local sympathisers, are actually descending from three directions.
One lot, still perhaps 500 km (300 miles) away, is coming from the northwest after taking the former garrison town of Kamina, cutting supply routes to diamond-rich Kasai province.
Another is coming due south from an area of scenic lakes and the closest column has taken the town of Kasenga, on Zambia's river border 200 km (120 miles) to the northeast.

No one expects the Zairean army -- unpaid and unsure what it would be fighting for -- to defend Lubumbashi, 1,800 km (1,100 miles) from the capital Kinshasa, fiercely independent and already mentally in the hands of Kabila, a local man.

But the troops may loot or riot as they flee -- or do worse if they are trapped by a phantom fourth column that, rumour alone has it, was nearing the city from the south and would thus block any escape route into Zambia.
"If you corner a snake, it will bite. If you just scare it, it will run away," said one concerned expatriate.

While the poor openly beg Kabila to come, few prominent people, nervous about their frustrating and protracted wait between the old order and the new, want to be seen talking, let along to have their names published.
Mobutu's feared SNIP security police are still around but Kabila's "fifth columnists" are also widely believed to be lying low inside Lubumbashi, just waiting for their moment.

Many of the city's 1,500 Belgian and other expatriate workers sent their families away for long Easter holidays until the storm had passed, but stayed on themselves to look after homes and businesses in a city ravaged before by looting.

"We are looking very closely at the situation in Shaba particularly because the fall of Lubumbashi seems to us to be imminent," a Belgian officer stationed in Congo, part of a paratroops force on standby to evacuate Belgians, told the Belgian RTL-TVI television on Thursday.
With each passing day, residents get jumpier in what was in Belgian colonial days known as Elisabethville.
All it takes is for someone to swear he's seen a rebel skulking in the tall grass that surrounds the city, or for a soldier to be seen running fast, for fear to take grip.
